title: Anxiety: When the Mind Stays on High Alert and How Balance is Restored
content:
Anxiety does not always look like panic. Sometimes, it looks like it is overthinking. Constant planning. The inability to relax even when everything seems fine. It looks like a mind that refuses to switch off, always scanning, always preparing, always anticipating what could go wrong.

For many people, anxiety feels like living in a state of “almost danger.” I once encountered an individual who described it in a way that was both simple and deeply accurate: “Nothing is happening, but my body feels like something is about to happen.”

He was functioning. He showed up to work, met deadlines, maintained relationships. But internally, his experience was very different. His thoughts moved rapidly, jumping from one worry to another. His chest often felt tight. His sleep was restless. Even in calm environments, his body remained tense. This was not just stress. It was anxiety. Clinically, anxiety is an emotional and physiological response to perceived threat. In normal situations, it serves as a protective function, helping the body prepare for danger. But when anxiety becomes persistent, excessive, or disconnected from actual threat, it begins to interfere with daily functioning.

The brain’s alarm system becomes overactive. At a biological level, anxiety involves heightened activity in the amygdala, the part of the brain responsible for detecting threats. This triggers the release of stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. The body prepares for action. Heart rate increases. Breathing becomes faster. Muscles tighten. Attention narrows.

This response is useful in real danger. But in anxiety, the system activates too often, sometimes without a clear cause. The individual I mentioned experienced this constantly. His mind would generate “what if” scenarios throughout the day. What if something goes wrong? What if I fail? What if something happens to someone I care about? These thoughts were not occasional. They were repetitive and intrusive.

Over time, his body began to mirror his thoughts. He felt fatigued, not because he lacked sleep, but because his system was always active. Rest did not feel restful. Even moments of stillness were filled with internal noise. One of the most important shifts came through understanding.

When he learned that his symptoms had a biological basis, that his body was responding to perceived threats even when none were present, he began to separate himself from the experience. Instead of seeing himself as “overreacting,” he began to see that his system was dysregulated. That awareness reduced self-judgment. From there, structured care focused on regulating both the mind and body. Sleep patterns were stabilized. Daily routines were adjusted to reduce constant overstimulation. Physical health was considered as factors such as caffeine intake, stress levels, and overall lifestyle can influence anxiety intensity. Medical support was introduced where necessary to calm the overactive response system. Progress was gradual. At first, he noticed small changes. His breathing became steadier. His sleep improved slightly. The intensity of his thoughts reduced, even if they did not disappear completely. Then, something more significant happened. He began to experience moments of quiet. Not complete silence, but gaps between the noise. Moments where his mind was not anticipating the worst. Moments where his body felt at ease. He later said, “For the first time, I feel like my body is not fighting something all the time.” That is what regulation feels like. Anxiety is not just in the mind. It is in the body, the breath, the nervous system, and the way a person relates to uncertainty. It affects concentration, decision-making, sleep, and overall quality of life. Left unmanaged, it can become chronic, shaping behavior and limiting experiences. People may begin to avoid situations that trigger discomfort, withdraw from opportunities, or remain in a constant loop of anticipation that drains their energy over time. But anxiety is manageable. The nervous system can be retrained. The brain can learn to differentiate between real and perceived threats. With consistent structure, informed care, and intentional regulation, the intensity of anxiety can reduce significantly.

One of the most important steps is recognition. Persistent worry, restlessness, muscle tension, difficulty sleeping, rapid thoughts, and a constant sense of unease are not just personality traits. They are signals that the system is overactivated and needs recalibration. Early attention prevents escalation. The goal is not to eliminate anxiety completely. A certain level of anxiety is necessary for survival and performance. The goal is balance, where the mind can respond to real challenges without remaining trapped in a constant state of alert. Because when the mind is no longer fighting imagined danger, it regains its capacity for clarity, presence, and rest.

And in that space, life becomes something to experience, not something to constantly prepare for.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu
(DNP, PMHNP, FNP)

title: STIs: The Conditions You Don’t Feel and the Power of Knowing Early
content:
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) rarely begin with alarm. There is no loud warning. No immediate disruption. No clear signal that something has changed. Most of the time, they begin in silence. I once encountered an individual who came in for what he described as “just a routine check.” There were no complaints. No discomfort. No visible signs that anything was wrong. From his perspective, his health was intact. The results told a different story. He was living with an infection he had no awareness of. No pain had alerted him. No symptoms had interrupted his daily life. Yet the infection had been present long enough to pose risks, both to his own health and to others. This is the reality of many sexually transmitted infections. They do not always announce themselves.

Clinically, STIs are infections caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites transmitted primarily through sexual contact. Common examples include chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and HIV. Each of these infections behaves differently in the body, but many share one critical feature in their early stages: they can be asymptomatic. This means a person can carry and transmit an infection without any noticeable signs.

Early detection allows for timely medical management, reducing the risk of complications and preventing further transmission. Prevention also plays a central role. Understanding how infections spread allows individuals to make informed decisions. Protective measures, open communication, and responsible practices significantly reduce risk.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu (DNP,PMHNP-BC,FNP-BC)

title: Depression: The Quiet Erosion and the Path Back to Self
content:
Depression rarely begins with collapse. It begins subtly. A slight loss of interest. A growing fatigue that rest does not fix. A quiet withdrawal from things that once felt meaningful. Many people cannot pinpoint when it starts. They only know that somewhere along the way, life began to feel heavier.

In clinical practice, I have learned that depression is not simply sadness. Sadness is an emotion. Depression is a medical and psychological condition. It alters how the brain processes mood, motivation, memory, sleep, appetite, and even physical sensation. It affects how a person interprets the past, experiences the present, and imagines the future.

One individual once described it this way: “It feels like I’m alive, but I’m not living.”

He was accomplished and responsible. He showed up to work. He paid his bills. He responded to messages. From the outside, nothing appeared wrong. But internally, he felt detached from his own existence. Activities that once excited him felt mechanical. Conversations required effort. Even joy felt distant, as though it belonged to someone else.

What he was experiencing was not weakness. It was a major depressive episode.

Clinically, depression can present with persistent low mood, diminished interest or pleasure in activities, significant changes in sleep patterns, appetite disturbances, low energy, impaired concentration, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, and in more severe cases, thoughts of death or hopelessness. For a diagnosis, these symptoms must persist for at least two weeks and cause noticeable impairment in daily functioning.

Depression reshapes cognition. It introduces distortions that feel convincing. The mind starts to whisper narratives such as “I am a burden,” “Nothing will change,” or “I am failing.” These thoughts do not feel like symptoms. They feel like truth.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu
DNP, PMHNP, FNP

title: Depression: When the Mind Turns Against Itself and How Restoration Begins
content:
Depression does not always look like tears. It looks like a high-performing executive who suddenly struggles to answer simple emails. It looks like a parent who loves their children deeply but feels emotionally absent. It looks like a young adult lying awake at 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, exhausted but unable to sleep. It looks like someone saying, “I’m just tired,” when what they truly mean is, “I don’t recognize myself anymore.”

Depression is not simply a low mood. It is a systemic shift in how the brain and body function.

I once worked with a man who described his experience as “a slow fading.” He could not identify a single catastrophic event that triggered it. Instead, he noticed gradual changes. Food lost its taste. Music sounded flat. Achievements felt hollow. Even laughter felt rehearsed.

Clinically, depression can present in multiple forms. Some individuals experience profound sadness and tearfulness. Others experience irritability, agitation, or emotional blunting. Many report persistent fatigue, slowed thinking, difficulty concentrating, disrupted sleep, appetite changes, feelings of worthlessness, and a heavy sense of hopelessness about the future.

At a biological level, depression is linked to disruptions in neurotransmitters such as serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These chemicals influence mood regulation, motivation, reward processing, and energy levels. When these systems are dysregulated, the world can feel colorless and effortful.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu
DNP, PMHNP, FNP

title: Bipolar Disorder: When the Mind Moves Between Extremes and the Science of Stability
content:
Bipolar disorder is one of the most misunderstood mental health conditions.

Many people assume it simply means “mood swings.” It is far more complex. Bipolar disorder involves significant shifts in mood, energy, thinking patterns, and behavior that go far beyond normal emotional changes. These shifts can move between periods of deep depression and periods of unusually elevated or energized mood known as mania or hypomania.

During one phase of his life, he felt unstoppable. Sleep seemed unnecessary. His mind produced ideas rapidly, and he believed he could accomplish anything. He worked through the night, started multiple projects at once, spoke with intense enthusiasm, and felt unusually confident about decisions that others questioned.

At first, the energy felt productive. He described it as clarity and brilliance. But as the state intensified, the acceleration became overwhelming. His thoughts raced faster than he could organize them. His sleep was reduced to only a few hours. His decision-making became impulsive.

This was not simply ambition or excitement. It was mania.

Yet bipolar disorder does not remain in that heightened state. Eventually, the mind shifts in the opposite direction.

The same individual who once felt unstoppable began to feel completely depleted. The ideas that once came effortlessly disappeared. The energy vanished. He struggled to wake up in the morning. Motivation disappeared, and a deep sense of hopelessness emerged.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu
DNP, PMHNP, FNP

title: Bipolar Disorder: Living Between Two Extremes and the Science of Regaining Balance
content:
Bipolar disorder is often misunderstood because people see only fragments of it. Some witness the high energy and assume it is simply enthusiasm or ambition. Others notice the deep withdrawal and believe it is just sadness or exhaustion. What many do not see is the full cycle, the dramatic movement between emotional extremes that can reshape a person’s thoughts, behavior, energy, and identity.

At its core, bipolar disorder is a disorder of regulation. The brain normally maintains a balance between activation and rest, motivation and calm, excitement and reflection. In bipolar disorder, that balance becomes unstable. The mind can accelerate far beyond normal levels of energy and confidence, and at other times it can descend into profound depression where even the simplest tasks feel impossible.

During certain periods, he felt electrified by life. Ideas flowed rapidly. His thoughts moved so quickly that conversations struggled to keep up with him. He slept only a few hours each night yet woke up feeling energized.

But what they did not see was how the acceleration gradually moved beyond control. His thoughts began to race faster than he could organize them. Sleep became almost nonexistent. His judgment shifted. He made impulsive decisions, spent money recklessly, and took risks he would normally avoid.

Dr. Oladunni Faminu
DNP, PMHNP, FNP
